claims.text: The Ir–Os–Pt–Pd–Rh–Ru catalyst can catalyze ethanol oxidation through a 12-electron process.
Ethanol oxidation on the catalyst involves both 12-electron and 12-proton transfers.
The target nanoscale PGM catalyst has unusually high activity, selectivity, and durability during ethanol oxidation.
The as-synthesized catalyst has a Pt-rich, highly dispersed configuration.
Adjacent Pt-group metal sites synergistically modulate the adsorption energies of ethanol and its intermediates.
An atomically mixed PGM ensemble creates a heterogeneous landscape of active sites with different local electronic structures.
The catalytically relevant ensemble is located particularly on a Pt-rich surface.
The active sites dynamically restructure under ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Dynamic restructuring produces an optimized binding-energy profile for ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Optimized intermediate adsorption enables effective conversion through the multistep 12-electron process.
The heterogeneous neighboring-site landscape suppresses unwanted side reactions and improves selectivity.
Synergistic interactions among adjacent PGM atoms alter the d-band structure.
Synergistic electronic interactions in multicomponent PGM materials can regulate adsorbate binding energies.
The proposed ensemble effect reduces poisoning of active sites.
The proposed ensemble effect suppresses catalyst dissolution.
Controlled thermal annealing will subtly alter atomic mixing, surface ordering, electronic interactions, and the distribution of adjacent active sites without significant particle growth.
Annealing will form or reorganize closely adjacent, under-coordinated PGM sites on a Pt-rich surface.
Relative to the as-synthesized baseline, annealing will lower the ethanol-oxidation onset potential and increase peak current density.
Relative to the as-synthesized baseline, annealing will reduce activity fade during extended potential cycling.
The adjacent-site synergy should be less pronounced at extreme potentials or in strongly acidic electrolytes because other pathways or deactivation modes may dominate.
